Update: This launch was originally scheduled for Nov. 13. ULA has now delayed it twice, first due to a power issue in the plant that provides gaseous nitrogen to Vulcan and then because of a communication problem between ground equipment and the rocket. Vulcan and its payloads remain healthy, according to ULA.

United Launch Alliance's (ULA) Vulcan Centaur rocket will fly on Sunday (Nov. 15) for the first time in nine months, and you can watch the action live.

A Vulcan Centaur topped with 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites is scheduled to lift off from Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Nov. 15 at 12:11 p.m. ET (1711 GMT).

You can watch it live here at Space.com, courtesy of ULA, or directly via the company. Coverage will start 20 minutes before liftoff.

Vulcan Centaur is the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket, which has just a half-dozen launches left on its manifest.

Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and has flown three more times since. On two of those missions — its second, in October 2024, and its fourth, in February of this year — the rocket experienced an issue with one of its solid rocket boosters (SRBs).

In both cases, an SRB nozzle burned through and fell off about 30 seconds after launch. Vulcan Centaur overcame the problem on both launches, successfully delivering its payloads to their designated orbits. But the U.S. Space Force was concerned enough that it decided to pause national security launches on Vulcan until ULA addresses the problem. (Vulcan's third and fourth launches were Space Force missions.)

ULA has been working hard on that front, and the company is confident that Vulcan is ready to return to flight.

"The integrated team has made great strides in improving our understanding of the SRB anomaly that occurred on the previous Vulcan flight and have identified several potential contributors, which have been mitigated through design and process improvements to the nozzle," the company said in an Oct. 28 update.

"To support our customers, this upcoming launch will utilize the improved nozzle design, and additional testing and analysis will continue in parallel with the mission," ULA added. "By flying the improved design, ULA gains valuable flight data that validates these improvements and is the most beneficial path in support of all our customers."

Sunday's launch will help build out Amazon's broadband constellation in low Earth orbit (LEO), which was previously called Project Kuiper but is now known as Amazon Leo. It will eventually compete with SpaceX's Starlink network, which has been up and running for several years.

Amazon Leo will eventually consist of more than 3,200 satellites. About 400 of them have reached space to date on 15 launches, which have been conducted by three different rockets — the Atlas V, SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6. Today's launch will be the first such mission for the Vulcan Centaur, which explains ULA's name for the launch — Vulcan Leo 1.

If all goes according to plan Sunday, Vulcan Centaur will deploy the 40 Amazon Leo satellites over a 25-minute span beginning about 70 minutes after launch. They'll be released roughly 270 miles (435 kilometers) above our planet.

The Amazon Leo launch will be part of a very busy stretch in spaceflight. SpaceX launched its Starship megarocket on Friday (Nov. 13), on a test mission that's on course to feature the first-ever catch attempt of the vehicle's Ship upper stage. And Rocket Lab launched its 100th-ever mission at 12:30 a.m. EST (0530 GMT) on Saturday (Nov. 14), sending a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite to orbit.

You can watch all of this action live here at Space.com when the time comes.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

"This is the critical breakthrough needed to make life multiplanetary."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Update for 6:25 p.m. ET: SpaceX has launched the Starship Flight 15 mission, but did skip the first stage Super Heavy booster landing. See launch video and our full Starship Flight 15 liftoff wrap.

Having reached orbit for the first time with Starship last time out, SpaceX is looking to take a huge stride toward full reusability with Flight 15 — the first attempt to catch the megarocket's Ship upper stage, as the company eyes hourly launches by 2030.

SpaceX is targeting today (Nov. 13) for Starship's 15th flight, which will lift off from the company's Starbas site in South Texas. If all goes well, the mission — which you can watch here at Space.com — will end on Saturday (Nov. 14) with the first attempt at what SpaceX itself calls the "Holy Grail of rocketry": Catching both Starship's Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage chopstick-style back at the launch pad.

"If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket," SpaceX wrote in its Flight 15 mission description.

The 75-minute Flight 15 launch window opens today at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT), and a number of Starship firsts are planned for early in the flight. For example, while SpaceX has caught three Super Heavy boosters and reused two of them to date, the first attempt to catch a next-gen Super Heavy "V3" vehicle will come today, around 6.5 minutes after liftoff.

If the Ship upper stage gets the go-ahead for orbital insertion, it will deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites — designed especially for use on Starship — into low Earth orbit (LEO), starting about 35 minutes after launch. Then, 21 hours later, if "internally developed, and FAA-approved, conditions" for a return to Starbase and catch are met — including on-orbit assessment of Ship's heat shield by three of the V3 satellites — SpaceX will attempt to recover the orbital upper stage.

This landmark try will follow the first-ever Ship reentry over inhabited areas, as the vehicle will maneuver its way over sparsely populated regions of northern Mexico and southern Texas. (On previous missions, Ship has splashed down in the open ocean.) It will head back to Starbase and make a bellyflop maneuver as it descends to the site's Pad 2 before flipping itself vertical, ready for embrace of the launch tower's waiting mechanical arms.

"SpaceX will attempt to catch both the Super Heavy booster and Starship on the upcoming flight. If both are successful, it will mark the first time that all parts of an orbital rocket return to Earth intact," Elon Musk said via X, the social media platform he owns, on Nov. 6. "This is the critical breakthrough needed to make life multiplanetary."

Half of the system is already proven. With catching and reflying boosters largely established, the next and unprecedented step is catching Ship. This is no easy task. The vehicle, returning from orbital speeds, must survive the heat of reentry, make its way precisely back to the pad put itself in position to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. The full recovery of an orbital launch system would, in the words of SpaceX, be a "breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket" and would open the "door to airplane-like cadence."

A successful catch would allow SpaceX to then work on refurbishing Ship for reflight, the next challenge of full reusability. Musk said in August in a SpaceX earnings call that the company will aim to refly the Super Heavy and Ship early next year.

SpaceX has a lot of experience with rocket reuse, as its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket pioneered the practice. But the company is eyeing another level of reflight with Starship: It's targeting roughly 10,000 launches of the megarocket per year by 2030, which works out to more than one launch per hour.

"We're aiming to reach 30+ Starship launches/day in 2030, which is ~10k annualized," Musk posted on X in August.

The company has repeated that figure to regulators. In comments filed with the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration in late October, it said that "SpaceX anticipates conducting 10,000 launches per year itself." Meanwhile, the recently signed National Space Transportation Policy aims to boost the U.S.'s capabilities to support more than 1,000 rocket launches per year by 2030.

Musk added that SpaceX's planned Starbase Louisiana site alone could support that many Starship launches. For context: SpaceX launched 165 Falcon 9 missions in 2025, and that was about half of the global total for orbital flights.

Why is SpaceX targeting this incredible increase in launch cadence? It wants to build satellite megaconstellations that dwarf anything the world has ever seen.

The company's V3 Starlink satellites are too large to fly efficiently on the Falcon 9. Each one of the next-gen spacecraft adds 1 terabit of capacity to SpaceX's broadband network, and the 26 flying on Flight 15 are equivalent to around 10 Falcon 9 launches packed with Starlink V2 Mini satellites, according to SpaceX. And the company wants to put a staggering 100,000 V3 Starlink satellites into orbit. (There are currently about 11,000 current-gen Starlink satellites in orbit, and that's by far the largest satellite network assembled to date.)

SpaceX's Starmind project blows even this figure out of the water. SpaceX wants to launch up to 1 million satellites to serve as orbital AI data centers, and it appears to be making the moves terrestrially regarding the hardware. On Nov. 10, German firm Singulus Technologies announced a contract worth more than 60 million euros for a solar cell production line for Starmind satellites, which SpaceX builds in Bastrop, Texas. Musk said the order covers equipment for 100 gigawatts of solar cells per year. In terms of orbital hardware, the project is only feasible if SpaceX can reach its targeted "airplane-like cadence."

The gap between SpaceX's vision and the situation today is vast. Starship flew four times in 2024 and five times in 2025, and Flight 15 would be its fourth launch of 2026. Musk said on the earnings call that he expects Starship to fly weekly at some point in the first half of 2027, and twice weekly or more by the end of that year. Starbase in Texas is currently authorized for 25 launches per year, and the Louisiana site is not expected to host a launch before 2029.

Even a perfect outing for Flight 15 and two clean catches will leave lots of work to do. SpaceX will then need to demonstrate reflight with Ship, after assessing the impact on its heat shield system. Then comes orbital refueling, which is a necessary step for any Starship trip beyond LEO and a requirement for SpaceX's commitment to NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. It's unclear how many tanker flights and refuelings will be needed to make a lunar mission possible, but, whatever the number, Starship will probably need to be rapidly reusable. Another step is carrying people. SpaceX has tested life support hardware on the ground in a crew cabin for the moon lander version of Starship that it is building for NASA, but no Starship has flown with such a system.

There are no guarantees for Flight 15. Ship will only be cleared for a return to Starbase and a catch attempt if it meets safety checks after reaching orbit, which itself is an achievement not to be taken for granted. Flight controllers may end up needing to bring Ship down in the Pacific Ocean or divert its reentry into the Gulf late into flight.

Musk told investors last month that success on this flight is "more likely than not." Whatever happens today and on Saturday, the measure of Starship's progress will soon shift from whether SpaceX can catch a Ship to how quickly it can launch one again.

#756. Richard Sterban, Oak Ridge Boys Bass Singer Who Helped Make ‘Elvira’ a Hit, Dies at 83

Known for his signature "oom poppa, mow mow" bass line on "Elvira," Sterban had 17 No. 1s on the Hot Country Songs chart with The Oak Ridge Boys, plus two top 40 hits on the all-genre Hot 100.

Richard Sterban, the bass vocalist behind the “oom poppa, mow mow” hook on one of The Oak Ridge Boys‘ biggest hits, “Elvira,” and whose career launched as a backing singer for Elvis Presley, died on Saturday (Nov. 14). He was 83.

Sterban passed away due to complications from bronchitis and pneumonia in Hendersonville, Tenn., his family shared. He died after a long battle with cancer, and after retiring from touring last year.

“We appreciate all of your love, support, and prayers,” the Sterban family said in a statement released on Saturday. “Please continue to lift us up in this difficult time. We find comfort knowing that he is currently face to face with Jesus.”

Sterban, a member of The Oak Ridge Boys for more than 50 years with Duane Allen, William Lee Golden and the late Joe Bonsall, revealed a pancreatic cancer diagnosis in September 2025, saying at the time that he was “under the care of the best cancer doctors in the country and, with the help of the Good Lord above, I believe I will be able to get through this.”

“Elvira” — The Oak Ridge Boys’ highest-charting single on the all-genre Billboard Hot 100, a song that became one of the quartet’s numerous No. 1s on the Hot Country Songs chart, and the winner of a trio of major awards (a Grammy Award, a CMA Award and an ACM Award) put Sterban’s deep vocal front and center in the hit’s chorus.

The Oak Ridge Boys had 47 entries on the Hot Country Songs chart, including 17 No. 1s that spanned 1978-90. They also had 39 entries on the Top Country Albums chart, including three No. 1s (Fancy Free in 1981, Bobbie Sue in 1982 and Deliver in 1984).On the all-genre Billboard Hot 100, the group notched four entries, including two top 40-charted hits: “Elvira” (No. 5 in 1981) and “Bobbie Sue” (No. 12 in 1982).

Sterban was born in Camden, N.J., in 1934, and grew up in nearby Collingswood, where he sang at Sunday school and in his seventh grade glee club. He went to Trenton State College, now The College of New Jersey, to study music.

Before his professional journey in music led him to The Oak Ridge Boys, Sterban helped found the gospel quartet The Keystones in the Philadelphia area; Bonsall, who would go on to join The Oak Ridge Boys with him, also sang in the group.

In the early 1970s, Sterban found himself singing as a backing vocalist for superstar Elvis Presley.

For more than a year, he performed with Elvis onstage with J.D. Sumner and the Stamps Quartet, who appeared in the concert film Elvis on Tour (1972).

By 1972 the opportunity to join The Oak Ridge Boys — then a gospel four-piece who hadn’t yet shifted to the sound that would make them a household name in country music — came. The group’s previous bass singer Noel Fox had departed. Sterban decided to take the gig.

Johnny Cash featured The Oak Ridge Boys on tour, and the quartet would go on to sign with Cash’s manager, Jim Halsey, who’s credited with encouraging them to get into country.

Throughout his decades-long career with The Oak Ridge Boys, Sterban won five Grammys, including the award for best country performance by a duo or group with vocal in 1982 for “Elvira,” which had already been named single of the year by both the Country Music Association and the Academy of Country Music.

Sterban’s deep voice was a centerpiece on the recording, which was penned by Dallas Frazier and produced by Ron Chancey.

“We looked at each other and said, ‘We think this is the song we’ve been looking for,'” Sterban recalled in a 2012 interview with Billboard timed around the release of his autobiography, From Elvis to Elvira. “To this day, I remember the look was on everybody’s faces in the studio. They all were having so much fun, and smiling. I remember Jimmy Capps was playing rhythm guitar, and he had such a grin on his face. I remember Ron telling me, ‘You need to sing that oom papa mow mow part,’ and on Dallas’ version, as well as the one by Kenny Rogers and the First Edition, the line was on there, but not as predominant. He said, ‘Take it and make it your own.'”

In later years, Sterban was inducted into the Philadelphia Hall of Fame, the Gospel Music Hall of Fame, the Vocal Group Hall of Fame and the Country Music Hall of Fame. The Oak Ridge Boys became members of the Grand Ole Opry in 2011.

In a statement emailed on Saturday, Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum CEO Kyle Young wrote, “Richard Sterban was a musical bridge builder. He used his unmistakable bass voice to connect commercial country music to its deep gospel roots. Growing up in New Jersey, a dream was born when he heard J.D. Sumner sing. Richard later joined J.D. and the Stamps Quartet, accompanied Elvis Presley onstage, and became a member of the Oak Ridge Boys in 1972. He helped the supergroup achieve seventeen #1 hits, legions of fans the world over, and a well-deserved place in the Country Music Hall of Fame. Like his signature vocal style, Richard Sterban was a steady force and a foundational figure in country music.”

Country Music Association CEO Sarah Trahern wrote, “Today we mourn the loss of an essential part of the quartet that has become a cornerstone of our genre. Richard’s deep bass not only defined the sound of The Oak Ridge Boys, but also brought warmth, soul, and character to every performance. His talent helped shape songs that became truly timeless. Our hearts go out to Richard’s friends and family during this difficult time.”

Of his time performing with The Oak Ridge Boys, in 2012 Sterban told Billboard, “We are a very unique group. If you look at the four of us, we are so different from each other — like night from day. But, there’s something magical and special about us as a foursome. I think we realize we need each other, and we are a true team. We still look forward to getting on stage every night and taking our music to the audiences. I think that’s very important.”

Oak Ridge Boys tenor vocalist Joe Bonsall died from complications of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) in 2024.

Sterban stepped away from performing live due in 2025 due to his health, but he did rejoin the current formation of the group to sing “Elvira” at the Grand Ole Opry on Jan. 30 and 31, 2026. He also sang on their 2026 album Buried Treasures, which arrived in October.

Sterban is survived by wife Donna; daughters Lauren (Tyler) and Tori (Mitchell); sons Rich (Chele), Doug, and Chris; grandchildren, Mali (Zachary), Nikolas, Tyler (Ryann), Madelyn, Alexandra, Rex, Owen, and Charli Grace and great-grandchildren Salem, Asher, and Theo. Funeral arrangements will be announced at a later date.

Navy veteran Suni Williams leads in a longstanding astronaut tradition.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

New Yorkers got a space-y surprise on Wednesday (Nov. 11): Retired NASA astronaut and U.S. Navy Captain Sunita "Suni" Williams rolled down 5th Avenue in the back of a classic convertible wrapped in patriotic decals as Grand Marshal of the Veterans Day Parade.

On Wednesday, New York City's 107th annual Veterans Day Parade made its way through Manhattan to the cheers and respectful nods of thousands of onlookers.

The parade is an annual tradition on the holiday, which honors veterans of the U.S. armed forces. As part of the parade, veterans, active-duty soldiers, firefighters, marching bands, youth cadets and more march through the city and honor those who have served and sacrificed in the U.S. military.

This year, the parade featured Suni Williams as its grand marshal. "I’m proud to join New Yorkers and Americans from around the country in honoring the service, sacrifice, and commitment of veterans from every generation," she said during the event.

Williams was selected for NASA's astronaut program in 1998 and retired from it in December 2025. She spent 608 days in space during her astronaut career, the second-most by an American astronaut behind Peggy Whitson, who racked up 695.

Williams also had an extensive career in the U.S. Navy. She began as an ensign in 1987 before serving in a number of different roles. For example, she was a diving officer and a naval aviator and also provided helicopter combat support during Operation Desert Shield and Operation Provide Comfort. She further served as a squadron safety officer and finally as a captain, a rank she achieved in 2017.

During this time, Williams supported relief efforts following Hurricane Andrew, trained within the U.S. Naval Test Pilot School and gained a wealth of further experience flying as a military pilot.

Williams is part of a longstanding tradition of astronauts serving in the U.S. military. From test pilots to naval officers and more, there's a strong link between the U.S. armed forces and NASA's astronaut program.

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. #753. Filipino Singer Carmelle Storms to Victory in Eurovision Asia Debut in Bangkok

The 19-year-old said her winning song celebrated female empowerment and was intended as "a tribute to all Filipino women."

Filipino singer Carmelle won the first Asian edition of the Eurovision Song Contest on Saturday (Nov. 14) with a fiery performance of her dance-pop song “Sobra-Sobra.”

The 19-year-old beat 10 other acts in the grand final in Bangkok, with the winner chosen through votes from national juries in participating countries and viewers worldwide.

After her victory, Carmelle said her song celebrated female empowerment and was intended as “a tribute to all Filipino women.”

“I made history, since this was the first time,” she told The Associated Press. “It’s such a big responsibility for me, because this one is a global stage, so thank you everybody who voted for me.”

Thai duo Mang x Daou finished second with an energetic performance of the romantic pop song “Aroma.” Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên placed third with a lively, stylish rendition of “Em Tiên.”

Malaysia’s Aina Abdul took fourth with her powerful ballad “Bluest Sky.” Thinla of Laos finished fifth with “Bae,” a playful dance track that had the audience dancing whenever it was replayed during the show.

Bhutan, South Korea, Mongolia, Nepal, Cambodia and Bangladesh also competed.

Contestants made their entrances aboard tuk-tuks, the motorized three-wheeled vehicles common in Bangkok’s tourist districts. They waved national flags as thousands of fans cheered inside the city-center venue.

Bulgarian singer Dara appeared as a special guest, performing “Bangaranga,” the song with which she won the 70th Eurovision Song Contest in Vienna earlier this year.

The European contest seeks to put music before politics but has repeatedly been caught up in international conflicts. Russia was expelled in 2022 following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The Israel-Hamas war in Gaza has also roiled the competition, prompting protests outside contest venues and leading organizers to restrict political flag-waving.

Five longtime participants — Spain, the Netherlands, Ireland, Iceland and Slovenia — boycotted this year’s European competition over Israel’s participation.

Eurovision Asia appeared less overshadowed by politics, said Eurovision historian Dean Vuletic, who attended the show in Bangkok.

He said an analysis of voting patterns might reveal political tendencies among participating countries.

“But for now I can say it was a very beautiful atmosphere inside the venue and it was a great window into the musical cultures of Asia.”

#752. Meet Plave, the Very Real Virtual K-pop Boy Group

As AI continues to push its way into the creative space, K-pop boy group Plave, powered by real performers and real artists, offers compelling and authentic counter-programming.

Plave, the chart-topping K-pop group, is similar to many other boy groups. They have intricate choreography, offer their dedicated fans a near-constant love online and an endless parade of stylish looks. But Plave has one major difference from other boy groups — they’re two-dimensional.

Hailing from Korean virtual entertainment company Vlast, Plave — comprising members Yejun, Noah, Bamby, Eunho and Hamin — has become a success story in what’s possible for a virtual group. The group utilizes real-time motion capture technology to display the five members, all real performers using a stage name, as cartoon-style avatars. Related Stories TV How to Stream the 2026 Latin Grammys Online 'Dancing' Diaries After 'DWTS' Season 35, Mark Ballas Would Love His Wife BC Jean to Be His Next Celebrity Partner

Hyunwoo Lee, Vlast’s CTO, explains that five years ago, the team made a venture company first, realizing that the real-time technology would likely get attention in the marketplace. “We weren’t the first company to leverage motion capture technology. Obviously, you might know that movie industry and game companies have been using motion capture a lot,” says Lee. Vlast, by their own admission, was the first to utilize it for real-time motion capture live streaming, however.

Live streams are ingrained in the fabric of the K-pop industry, that’s nothing new. Plave live streams often find them interacting with fans and chatting away. As with any technology, glitches are possible. Being first, as Lee explains, means they’re also the first to experience and troubleshoot these challenges. But fans have taken to clipping the moments and posting them online, which has only helped the group gain more virality.

Speaking with the members of Plave, displayed on a Zoom with The Hollywood Reporter by their avatar, is much like speaking with any other K-pop idol group. They’re excited to talk about their latest EP Hyperdrive, which debuted at No. 31 on the Billboard 200, their highest to date, and their upcoming U.S. concerts, landing tonight (Nov. 14) in Pasadena. The album, an EDM-based dance pop is a new genre for the group, and it’s one they’re excited to show off.

One of the many ways Plave bucks the norm in K-pop is in their formation. Unlike most groups in K-pop, formed through a years-long trainee process and handpicked by executives to make a final lineup, Plave was formed organically. “We’re actually friends,” says blue-haired Yejun. After meeting, they decided to give the group a try.

The members of Plave all have a hand in creating their music and choreography. Yejun, Noah and Eunho create songs for the group, while Bamby and Hamin create choreography. There’s no artificial intelligence involved in any of the group’s output, whether that be creatively or visually. “The look and feel of our members, their movements and the original looks that we show to our fans — those images are not generated by AI at all,” says Lee.

The group has long worked to prove themselves, perhaps having to work just a little harder given the knee-jerk reactions a virtual group might evoke. “Last year, we had our Asia tour, and after that I think we actually proved ourselves as a group,” says group member Noah.

“Being an artist is both a blessing and a curse,” Eunho says. “We are so grateful to be able to share our music with people, but at the same time, we always want to do better and show them something new.”

But the pressure to be better than before is what has kept the group going. It’s also helped them move into a global space they hadn’t before. In Asia, Plave is now a stadium act, recently performing two nights at Seoul’s Incheon Munhak Main Stadium. The concerts utilize large LED screens, immersing fans in the world of the group in ways 3D groups might not even be able to.

“[The tour] this year is reaching a more global and wide audience,” says the pink-haired Bamby. “It’s actually a very precious opportunity to meet fans all over the world that weren’t able to reach us.”

Hamin agrees. “The L.A. concert will be our last destination to wrap up our world tour,” he says. “I hope this actually resonates with our global audience.”

The company is coy about the logistics behind a concert day, but it’s safe to assume they continue to utilize that real-time motion capture. No matter how that will happen, the group is excited for more personal interactions with their fans. “We’ve been continuously closely communicating with our fans since our debut, says Noah.

He adds, “We’ve actually accumulated a lot of stories and experiences with them. We’re really close with them, going beyond family members.”

#750. BTS & ROSÉ Lead a Big Night for K-Pop at 2026 Kids’ Choice Awards: Full Winners List

Bruno Mars won favorite male artist for the second year in a row. Sombr and KATSEYE took the "breakout" awards.

Kids love K-Pop. That was abundantly clear from the results at the 2026 Kids’ Choice Awards, which aired on CBS for the first time on Saturday (Nov. 14). BTS won three major awards, though they weren’t at Television City in Hollywood for the taping, nor did they accept any of their awards by video, as ROSÉ and “global girl group” KATSEYE did.

BTS won favorite group for a record-extending fifth time; favorite song (“Swim”) for a second time and favorite album (ARIRANG) for the first time. In the favorite song category, BTS had won five years ago for “Dynamite.” The only other group or duo to win twice in the category is One Direction (back-to-back awards in 2013-14 for “What Makes You Beautiful” and “Story of My Life”). (The Kids’ Choice Awards originated in 1987.)

ROSÉ became the first K-Pop star to win favorite female artist. She beat, among others, Ariana Grande, who has won a record five times in this category; Taylor Swift, who has won three times; and Miley Cyrus, who has won twice.

ROSÉ’s Blackpink colleague JENNIE shared the award for favorite music collaboration with Tame Impala for their smash “Dracula.”

KPop Demon Hunters also won multiple awards. “Golden” won favorite song from a movie (beating Swift’s “I Knew It, I Knew You” from Toy Story 5, among others). The actors who voiced Rumi and Jinu in that movie won for favorite female and male animated voices from a movie, respectively.

Alex Warren was a good-natured host of the fast-paced show, which ran just 90 minutes. In one quick bit, he was costumed like a janitor, mopping up the slime. Only a dozen of the many awards were presented on the show. The producers program the show with the winners who were willing and able to appear. If you watched the show, you would have had no idea that BTS had a big night.

Nor would you have known that Bruno Mars won favorite male artist for the second year in a row; that Sombr won favorite new male artist; or that Olivia Dean‘s “Man I Need” took favorite viral song. “Man I Need” is expected to be a top contender for record and song of the year at the 2027 Grammy Awards.

KATSEYE won favorite female breakout artist/group. Bini, a Filipino girl group, won favorite global music star.

Several music performances brightened the show. Ashe performed her current top 30 Hot 100 hit, “Stop the Wedding!,” wearing a beautiful wedding gown, with her hair perfectly coiffed. No matter: She was doused with slime at the end of the performance like just about everyone else.

Jamie Miller performed “Babydoll,” which has been No. 1 on the Official U.K. Singles Chart for four weeks and is climbing the Hot 100. Sofi Tukker performed “Tsunami.” JYT performed briefly at the end of the opening segment, which focused on dance hits over the decades, stretching back to the 1980s. (The 1970s are now officially ancient history to today’s kids.)

A few other music and music-adjacent stars were enlisted as presenters, including Stella Lefty (who was slimed), Ice Spice and Teyana Taylor. TV veteran Keke Palmer looked around the fancy set and made a knowing comment: “I’ve watched a lot of Kids’ Choice Awards. Y’all have some money this year. I see you, CBS.”

Spider-Man: Brand New Day won favorite movie, and its stars, Tom Holland and Zendaya, won favorite movie actor and actress, respectively.

Howie Mandel accepted America’s Got Talent’s award for favorite TV show reality competition. He got off a funny line, saying his castmates were supposed to be there too, and were supposed to fly to Los Angeles on Friday. He feigned confusion as to why they didn’t make it, saying he even emailed them on Thursday to remind them. Yes, we’ve had a rough week.

Chris Pratt received the King of Comedy Award. He opened his remarks with a funny line. “My four kids were the greatest thing that ever happened to me – until tonight,” eyeing the miniature orange blimp he received. “This is the closest I’ll ever get to an Oscar. When I was a kid, I got in trouble for making kids laugh and now I’m getting an award for it.”

The show was rated PG, which is hard to imagine. If this wasn’t G-rated entertainment I don’t know what is. Yes, there was an ocean of slime, but the messaging was consistently positive, as when Pratt said that jokes can make people laugh, but they can also hurt people and that “kind comedy is the best kind of comedy.”

#749. This AI ‘mechanic’ can peer inside the black box of other neural networks

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Some AI models behave like mechanics — fixing issues in other models that they neither designed nor fully understand. Credit: Mint Images/Getty

Researchers have used an artificial-intelligence model to read and tinker with the internal workings of another AI network — offering a new way to peek into the ‘black box’ of AI.

Computer scientists usually improve models by training them in tiny increments or by building them from scratch. A team at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge has demonstrated how an AI model called GPT-6 Astra can interpret the raw internal values of some other models well enough to predict what different parts of the systems do. It can then edit the models to make improvements — including boosting their mathematical abilities. The authors reported their findings in a preprint1 on 2 November.

ChatGPT is a black box: how AI research can break it open

ChatGPT is a black box: how AI research can break it open

Frontier AI models are “showing early sparks” of an ability to treat neural networks like files that they can read, reason about and change, says co-author Rikiya Takehi, a machine-learning researcher at MIT.

The results do not mean that Astra, developed by OpenAI in San Francisco, California, can explain or understand how a given AI network works. But the findings suggest that general-purpose AI models — such as ChatGPT or Claude — might be able to modify a network in useful ways, like a mechanic who can identify and fix issues in an engine that they neither designed nor fully understand.

Researchers already try to interpret how different components of a network create its outputs. The preprint shows that it is possible to automate some of these ‘interpretability’ methods, says Fazl Barez, an AI-safety researcher at the University of Oxford, UK.

Researchers hope that better understanding models in this way will help to create safer AI systems, although Barez cautions that this assumption is “largely untested”.

It remains unclear if Astra is going beyond applying information and techniques learned in its training. Barez says he would be surprised if Astra is able to read and interpret models in ways that go beyond existing human abilities.

Three reasons why AI is not conscious and perhaps never will be

Three reasons why AI is not conscious and perhaps never will be

Still, if developed further, such ability to reprogram models might be an asset in developing AI for science, says Marinka Zitnik, a computer scientist and bioinformatician at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts. For example, it could help to spot errors in a model ahead of real-world testing, she says.

Frontier AI systems are based on massive neural networks — brain-inspired architectures in which layers of processing units, or neurons, are linked by billions of ‘weights’, values that represent the strength of connections inside a model. The strength of each weight is slowly nudged during training to make the model better at, for example, predicting a protein structure or the next word in a sentence.

The complex way in which a model’s features link to its outputs means they are often described as black boxes. Interpretability researchers run experiments to work out, for example, which weights are activated under specific conditions. Researchers have also previously developed custom models that can learn to edit other models2.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03679-8

Takehi, R., Teoh, J., Zhang, A. & Khattab, O. Preprint at alphaXiv https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2611.weight-space-programming (2026).

Schmidhuber, J. Neural Comput. 4, 131–139 (1992).

The StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian is a great model to learn the basics of manual telescope operation and get great views of your chosen targets, thanks to intuitive smartphone integration, but it isn't as easy to set up as you might think.

Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

Saturn was only a night past its annual opposition when I pointed the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian straight at it. The planet was at its biggest and brightest of the year, the seeing was good and its famous rings were visibly opening up after appearing edge-on from Earth in recent years. It was an obvious target for a new telescope.

Finding it took seconds. After selecting Saturn in Celestron’s StarSense Explorer app, I followed the on-screen arrows as I moved the telescope across the sky. As I got closer, the app zoomed in until a bullseye turned green. I looked through the supplied 25mm eyepiece, then swapped to the 10mm to see a pale yellow Saturn at 75x magnification, with its rings sharply defined and its giant moon Titan visible in orbit.

It was a stunning view, and exactly the kind of experience a beginner needs from a first telescope. There was no frustration and no wondering whether I was looking in the right place. StarSense took me straight there — but, crucially, I moved the telescope myself. I’ve always liked that combination of hand-holding and DIY observing that Celestron’s StarSense tech gives you.

I’m less convinced by the tabletop telescope it’s attached to. Although this $599 RRP (£379) model is significantly smaller than the Celestron StarSense Explorer 8-inch Dobsonian telescope I’ve previously reviewed, it still weighs 25 lbs (11.33 kg). You need to place it on something sturdy before you can use it comfortably. After living with it in my backyard, I’m not convinced the tabletop format is the advantage it initially appears to be.

I’ve used Celestron’s StarSense Explorer system on a variety of telescopes and have always been impressed by how easy this type of smartphone navigation is to use. The technology works just as well here and, for me, it remains one of the best ways of making a traditional optical telescope accessible to a complete beginner.

This isn’t a computerized GoTo telescope. There are no motors to slew across the sky automatically and no tracking system to keep an object centered. Instead, a smartphone sits in a dock attached to the telescope, and its camera looks at the sky via a small mirror. Celestron’s StarSense Explorer app analyzes the reflections of the stars it sees, works out exactly where the telescope is pointing and tells you which direction to push it to reach the object you want to observe.

My iPhone 16 Pro Max fitted perfectly into the dock, and the initial alignment process was identical to what I’d used before. Once that was done, I used StarSense to find the Pleiades (M45), the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), the Double Cluster in Perseus and Saturn. It worked every time, with the target appearing in the eyepiece when the app told me I had reached it.

I can find all of those objects without an app, but that’s not really the point. Beginners often struggle to translate a star chart or an astronomy app into actual telescope movements. StarSense gives you confidence that you’re heading in the right direction while still requiring you to operate it physically.

That makes it a useful way to learn the night sky. After repeatedly pushing the telescope from one familiar object to another, you begin to understand how everything fits together. That’s very different from pressing a button and watching a GoTo or smart telescope move itself, and it’s why I think StarSense is worth paying extra for, even on a relatively wide-field telescope like this one.

The StarSense system may be the headline feature, but the reason to buy any Dobsonian is aperture. This one uses a 150mm (5.9-inch) parabolic primary mirror with a 750mm focal length and a relatively fast f/5 focal ratio. That combination gives it fairly low-power, wide-field views that are particularly well suited to large star clusters.

The Pleiades was one of my favorite views. At 30x through the supplied 25mm eyepiece, the telescope gave me a sharp field of stars and a particularly good view of what I call “Carter’s Whip” — the curving line of stars running through the cluster. I saw little obvious softness towards the edges, and focusing was straightforward.

The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) was a different proposition. From my light-polluted backyard, I could see Andromeda’s bright core, but not its outskirts or its satellite galaxies. That’s largely a consequence of observing a galaxy from a city, not a criticism of a 150mm telescope, but it’s a useful reminder of what visual astronomy is actually like. Don’t expect the colorful, detailed views of galaxies and nebulas you see in astrophotos, such as the stacked images a smart telescope can give you.

Saturn was more rewarding, but I would have liked more magnification when the seeing was this good. Add a Barlow lens if planets are a priority — it can double the magnification of any eyepiece you use it with.

Overall, I was impressed by the telescope’s optics. The views were sharp and contrast-y, and there’s enough aperture here to make a serious start in visual astronomy. However, the two supplied 25mm and 10mm Kellner eyepieces are decidedly entry-level — and obvious candidates for upgrading in the medium term.

The focuser is a weak point. It’s a fairly basic 1.25-inch rack-and-pinion design, but I noticed some wobble and vibration while using it. That’s a shame because the focuser is one of the parts of a telescope you constantly interact with, and something smoother and more precise would make the entire instrument feel more accomplished.

The tabletop design isn’t necessarily as convenient as it sounds. I expected this scope to feel considerably more convenient than Celestron’s 8-inch StarSense Dobsonian. The base has built-in grab handles, but the assembled telescope's shape and weight make it awkward to lift onto a table — I certainly wouldn’t recommend it to anyone with a bad back. You could move the optical tube and base separately, but that starts to cancel out the convenience of owning a relatively compact tabletop telescope.

You also need to choose your table carefully. It has to be sturdy enough not to introduce vibrations, but not so large that you have to stretch across it to reach the eyepiece as the telescope points to different parts of the sky. I found myself bending and stretching into some awkward positions.

Once it’s in position, the Dobsonian mount worked well. The balance was good, and I didn't need to adjust the altitude tension, while the movements offered a useful mix of resistance and fluidity as I followed StarSense around the sky. At 75x, however, keeping Saturn centered was more difficult than I expected. It was easy to over-nudge the telescope, then correct in the opposite direction.

Celestron sells an optional tripod for the telescope, and after using the tabletop base, I can see why that might be attractive. However, I’d personally rather put the money towards a larger Dobsonian whose base is designed to sit directly on the ground.

This scope doesn’t arrive in one piece. Assembly took about 90 minutes, and it required all manner of screws and screwdrivers. The main problem was getting the screws into the holes in the Dobsonian base, which took so much effort that I ended up with a blister on my hand. That’s not what I expected from a telescope aimed at beginners, especially when almost everything about using it has been designed to make things easy.

Once built, things improved considerably. My review sample arrived well collimated, so I didn’t have to adjust the mirror alignment. The tube rings, phone dock and general construction were all good enough for a telescope at this price, and nothing about the telescope felt particularly fragile. Once the telescope is outside, on a suitable table and aligned, it’s an impressively straightforward instrument to use.

The more I used the StarSense Explorer 150mm Dobsonian, the more I wondered who really benefits from the tabletop format. It’s certainly smaller than Celestron’s 8-inch StarSense Explorer Dobsonian, but it’s still a substantial object to store, and I didn’t feel any more inclined to grab it for a quick observing session.

Going bigger offers an optical advantage. An 8-inch/203mm aperture collects about 83% more light than a 150mm aperture, which matters when you’re observing faint deep-sky objects. The 8-inch StarSense also had a much nicer 2-inch Crayford focuser, and generally felt like a telescope with a little more room to grow into.

Dobsonians are the perfect companion to smart telescopes. The latter have completely changed what beginners can photograph from their backyards, particularly under light pollution. They can reveal galaxies and nebulas that are extremely difficult or impossible to see visually. I use them all the time. But they are no substitute for navigating to and actually seeing objects in the night sky with your own eyes.

The two approaches don’t need to compete. A smart telescope has to be pointed and then left alone for an hour or four to stack images. That time could be spent pushing something like the StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian around the sky, and actually looking through an eyepiece at the same objects. One shows you far more than your eyes can detect, but the other lets you see the photons yourself — and make a human connection with the night sky.

At $599 RRP (£379), the StarSense Explorer 150mm sits in an interesting part of the beginner telescope market. There are smaller tabletop Dobsonians like the Celestron Moon Mission 100mm without smartphone navigation, but I think StarSense is worth paying extra for, particularly for a first-time telescope owner.

If you mainly want to observe planets and the moon, a refractor like the Celestron StarSense Explorer LT 70AZ also makes sense. However, if you want to go relatively large, I do recommend the StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian — with an important qualification. Its optics are good, StarSense is superb, and it’s an excellent way for a beginner to learn their way around the night sky, but I’m not convinced that 150mm is the sweet spot for this particular design. It’s too big to feel genuinely convenient as a tabletop telescope, yet not big enough to deliver the full advantages of a larger Dobsonian.

If space is tight, this is a very capable first telescope. If you have room for the 8-inch StarSense Explorer, I’d go bigger.

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

#745. Philomena Cunk Comes for Hollywood

Diane Morgan, who plays the daft documentary presenter, and creator Charlie Brooker discuss making 'Cunk on Cinema' — and letting interview subjects in on the joke.

Philomena Cunk is the star of two previous Netflix shows and has more than a decade of appearances on various BBC programs. So one would think that the people she interviews would have caught on to the bit by now.

And, in fact, they have — because the people behind Cunk, the confidently clueless documentary presenter played by Diane Morgan, have never fully hidden what they’re doing. “We’ve always been up front with the experts that this is a joke,” says Charlie Brooker, who created the character in his 2010s BBC show Charlie Brooker’s Weekly Wipe. “We’ve never been in the business of pranking them — we’ve always said so from the very beginning.” Related Stories TV 'Cunk on Cinema' Review: Michael Bay and Benedict Cumberbatch Join Diane Morgan's Documentary Presenter for Her Latest Laugh-Filled Netflix Series Movies Aaron Pierre Starrer 'Fairytale in New York' Lands at Netflix

That subjects go into an interview with Philomena Cunk knowing it’s a comedy show — and then still get caught completely off guard by her inane lines of questioning, malapropisms and tangents about other people in her life — is a testament to how well Morgan plays the character, who never breaks her deadpan demeanor.

“I don’t think it really matters, does it?” Morgan tells The Hollywood Reporter about subjects knowing what they’re getting into. “Because they don’t know what questions they’re going to be asked.”

Morgan’s ability to disarm interviewees, and her delivery of very joke-dense narration and on-camera exposition, are on full display in Cunk on Cinema, a follow-up to previous Netflix shows Cunk on Earth and Cunk on Life. It premieres Nov. 15 on Netflix (and the BBC in the U.K. and Ireland) and sends Philomena on a run through the history of film, featuring interviews with Benedict Cumberbatch, Michael Bay, screenwriter Steven E. de Souza and a number of film historians and academics.

Morgan and Brooker (best known in the U.S. as the creator of Black Mirror) talked with THR about the character’s origins, choosing film as the next subject for Philomena, and the importance of Technotronic’s “Pump Up the Jam” to the Cunk canon. (This interview has been edited and condensed.)

It’s amazing to me that people know you’re playing a character and you’re still able to get the kinds of reactions you do from them.

DIANE MORGAN They don’t get to meet me out of character. I just turn up in the suit and sit down. I don’t make them feel comfortable. The atmosphere is very tense, and it goes on for ages. And obviously, the crew try not to laugh. So even if one of us says something funny, [the interviewee] might not notice that it’s funny in the moment because no one’s laughing. It just flies past. So they seem to panic a little bit that it’s not working. But I can see there are definitely bits that are working. They just don’t feel like they’re working in the moment, because it feels very dead and terrifying.

CHARLIE BROOKER We’ve always been up front with the experts that this is a joke. We’ve never been in the business of pranking them. We’ve always said from the very beginning when we started doing [the character]. It was called “Moments of Wonder,” the strand that that was within Weekly Wipe. In the very first one of those, there’s one of my favorite moments ever. A man is very earnestly explaining how time works scientifically, and you [Diane], while he’s talking, turn around and look down the lens, like really bored and upset to be there, having to listen to this.

We had to tell that guy — we told him that was going to happen [and to] keep going. So they’re primed. They know that that Philomena is Diane, and they know that this is a comedy show. What they don’t know in any way what we’re going to ask them, and we can’t see quite where it’s gonna go. We’re not like Borat and [other] things that are using the prank format to expose something in the interviewee. We’re actually celebrating experts in a way. The joke for us is always on Philomena.

Can you talk a little more about the character’s origin? She’s been in a lot more things that people outside the U.K. might not have seen.

MORGAN It started in little two-minute sections [on Weekly Wipe]. They were TV reviews that I would do with another character called Barry Shitpeas [played by Al Campbell], where we would just review things, and it went well. I was told that it might not go well because everyone loves Charlie, and they don’t like anything that isn’t Charlie. So I was sort of terrified that there was going to be a huge backlash. But they were very nice. It’s a nice way to test out a character. You don’t often get the luxury of doing that.

BROOKER Diane is so naturally funny that at some point we went, “We could give this character a wider thing to do.” We thought, could we give Philomena her own mini inspiring documentary thread in the show? Then we thought maybe she could also interview real experts. The very first subject you did was time, which is quite a big topic.

MORGAN It was complete ripoff of physicist Brian Cox’s documentary that had just gone out. It’s always good to spoof something. You’ve got a template for something; now just take the piss out of the whole thing.

BROOKER I think we pitched a weekly show that was just Philomena [to the BBC], and they were like, we can’t quite commit to that yet. But we’ve got a season of shows coming up because it was the anniversary of Shakespeare’s [death]. They said why don’t you try doing Cunk on Shakespeare as a one-off? So we did that, and that then set the template for the show as a whole.

Are there specific people that inform how you portray her, or is it just more the conventions of documentary presenting?

MORGAN It’s sort of me if I had no social skills, but also, I can use all those tropes that other documentary makers use. They all do the same things. They all walk in the same way. They all use their hands in the same way. They all structure a sentence in the same way. They all go on a journey. You can use all that. It’s basically me, but taking the piss out of presenters.

How did you decide on the history of film for her next topic?

BROOKER We’d done Shakespeare, the history of Britain, the history of the Earth, and then we did Cunk on Life, which like the meaning of life and philosophy and biology. We were slightly like, well, what else is there?

Initially, we had a couple of competing thoughts. One was to do a travelog across America. There was going to be lots of stuff for the anniversary of you guys kicking our asses, but then we thought actually there’ll be too much of that around. So we reserved the right to do that [another time]. Then we were thinking about the arts — could we do Cunk on art and film and music? If you do film, not only is there a lot to talk about, but there are a lot of highbrow documentaries about cinema that are treated with such reverence. It’s a different thing from doing history. It’s a different type of expert you’re going to get, and it’s a different bit of audience awareness. The more we talked about it, the more we thought that’s actually a really fruitful topic.

MORGAN It can be quite pretentious as well. That’s what excites me about it.

Diane, do you need to do a lot of prep work in order to get everything down in in the deadpan Philomena style, or has it kind of become second nature to you now?

MORGAN There’s more prep in the interview sections, because I like to try and second guess what they’ll ask me in case they ask me something, which they often do. The pieces to camera, I’m used to that now. People say, “Oh, you’re very deadpan.” But I think that’s just my face. If I don’t animate it, it just doesn’t do much. It looks quite sad. So that’s quite easy for me, the face thing and the voice thing.

In Cunk on Cinema, it seemed like there was a point where Benedict Cumberbatch started to improvise a little bit in your interview. But some of the other folks, like Steven E. de Souza and Michael Bay seemed a little more caught out by the absurdity of some of your questions.

BROOKER Steven de Souza, I think, was one of the ones who agreed really quickly [to be on the show]. He was very familiar with the character, and I think he said something like, “I’m a Cunk head,” so he was definitely on board. He absolutely got the assignment in that he was earnestly bemused by how he’s going to answer these questions. He seems genuinely flummoxed. Michael Bay, I think you were saying, maybe didn’t fully get your accent a lot of the time.

MORGAN I think he had a bit of trouble with the accent. One of my first questions was, “How much did your trainers cost?” And of course, you call trainers sneakers, don’t you?

So maybe he was thinking of a personal trainer or something?

MORGAN Yeah. There were a few that he was just like, “I don’t know what you’re saying.” But even that is funny, isn’t it? Someone just admitting they don’t know what the hell you’re talking about.

I want to ask a couple questions just about the whole Cunk project. First are the recurring references to “Pump Up the Jam.” Where did that idea come from, and why that particular song?

BROOKER In Cunk on Britain, we had a running joke where it was [cutaways to] Brush Strokes, a British sitcom from the 1980s which had a theme song by Kevin Rowland of Dexy’s Midnight Runners. We would show the opening sequence of Brush Strokes almost in full.

When we did Cunk on Earth, it was a co-production with Netflix, and we thought people outside Britain aren’t going to know what the hell Brush Strokes is. What could we possibly replace it with? I can’t remember where the suggestion of “Pump Up the Jam” came from, but it was kind of perfect.

MORGAN I love it. I didn’t appreciate it at the time.

[Editor’s note: There’s a bit more talk about the song and a novelty cover version that’s also used in Cunk on Cinema.]

BROOKER Then there are the captions that come up that get OK’d by Technotronic.

BROOKER Oh yeah. It’s part of the licensing deal, as I understand it. I may be wrong, but I think someone at Technotronic Towers …

BROOKER …has to look at these and go, “Yes, OK.”

MORGAN [Laughs] “Yeah, that’s fine, I like that.” Oh my god, that’s great. I didn’t know that.

BROOKER So there’s still somebody managing the jam pump.

Lastly, I just want to know if Philomena’s mate Paul is getting the help he needs.

MORGAN [Laughs] God, I love those Paul bits. They’re one of my favorite bits. Some people say, “Will he ever make an appearance?” But I don’t think you should ever see him, should you? It’s one of those characters — unless it’s Paul McCartney.

BROOKER I dream of getting Cunk to interview Paul McCartney. He’s had quite a life, hasn’t he, her mate Paul? His autobiography would be amazing.

MORGAN You could write that. People would buy it.

BROOKER It’s one of my favorite bits. There’s a really good one in this. I quite like it when there’s a Paul anecdote that goes on for far too long. There’s a good one to Michael Bay, who was very patient. Do people react differently when they hear that coming now, the interviewees?

MORGAN I think they do. I think there’s a [feeling of], “She’s mentioning Paul!” They’re getting the full experience.

Dreaming of a bright and shiny future filled with personal jet packs, levitating autos, and automated gadgets straight out of "The Jetsons?" Add in a gritty mystery, a notorious private eye, double-crossing aliens, and a bombshell diva framed for a killing, and you’ve got the perfect recipe for "Ray Gunn."

Oscar-winning director Brad Bird ("The Incredibles," "Ratatouille") returns to our screens with his new big-budget animated sci-fi project, "Ray Gunn," and this latest trailer has us primed.

"In Metropia, a gigantic city in an alternate future as seen from 1939, private eye Raymond Gunn (Sam Rockwell) is drawn into a case involving aliens, murder, and a multimedia starlet named Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson)," states the official synopsis.

Netflix Films and Skydance Animation's "Ray Gunn" is a stylistic pastiche of classic film noir tropes populated by down-and-out detectives and femme fatales living in the inspiring air of technological optimism viewed through a pre-war America lens.

Think "The Fifth Element" meets "Who Framed Roger Rabbit?" and "The Maltese Falcon," and you’re going to be close to this sci-fi whodunnit's vibe, which is intended for more mature audiences and rated PG.

This energetic new preview is locked and loaded with dazzling visuals by Cinesite, freaky creatures, streamlined flying cars, and a blistering pace. And if you listen very closely, The B-52s' "Planet Claire" can be heard playing in the background, which is one of the touchstones that inspired Bird to begin his 36-year journey to bring "Ray Gunn" to life. Was it worth the wait? We'll have to find out.

Also starring the vocal talents of Tom Waits, Bobby Cannavale, Alan Tudyk, Matt Berry, and Michelle Rodriguez, "Ray Gunn" opens in select theaters and 70mm screenings Dec. 4. After that, it lands on Netflix on Dec. 18... a date you might want to circle on your calendar, as that’s also the release slot for "Avengers: Doomsday" and "Dune: Part 3."

It's going to be a busy day for sci-fi fans. "Strap in, buster!"

#743. Hoobastank, Simple Plan and More Bands Performed Mid-Flight During Nationwide Air Travel Ground Stop

Southwest Airlines brought back its “Live at 35” program during Friday’s nationwide grounding of air travel with performances from artists on their way to Vans Warped Tour.

Hoobastank, The Used, Simple Plan and Lolo performed aboard a Southwest flight from Los Angeles to Orlando, Fla., on Nov. 13 as part of the music program, which hosts surprise midflight pop-up performances. The flight left Los Angeles around 11 a.m., about two hours before the FAA declared a national ground stop that snarled global travel and left more than 1 million people stranded. Related Stories Martin Scorsese Says His 'Cleopatra' Movie With Angelina Jolie Was 'Ruined' by Seth Rogen and the Sony Hack: 'It Was Gonna Be Really Wild' Seth Rogen on ‘The Invite,’ ‘Tangles,’ ‘The Studio’ Season 2, Reviving ‘Darkwing Duck’ and Why ‘Any A--hole Can Write That Joke’ Was the Best Advice He Ever Got

Hoobastank took to the aisles at cruising altitude for a live rendition of their 2004 hit “The Reason.” Passengers sang along and posted about the performance on social media. Lolo, who played at Warped Tour’s Long Beach, Calif., stop in July, wrote “Every plane was grounded today, but the emo gods made sure this one flew.”

The sky-high performance came amid a nationwide ground stop for all flights, with the Federal Aviation Administration citing “extraordinary circumstances.” The initial alert came just after 1 p.m. PT on Friday, stranding some 1.5 million travelers by CNN’s estimate. Airborne flights were allowed to continue, but new domestic flights were delayed or canceled, throwing travel plans into question for various industry events over the weekend. The stop was lifted about five hours later, shortly before 6 p.m. PT.

The “Live at 35” artists were in route to the final Vans Warped Tour 2026 stop in Orlando, which runs Nov. 14-15 at Camping World Stadium Campus. The Warped Tour expanded from three to five locations in 2026, with two-day festivals in Washington, D.C., Long Beach and Orlando, Fla. alongside two new international sites in Montreal and Mexico City.

Founded in 1995, Vans Warped Tour has become a definitive rock and alt festival, featuring 100+ artists across rock, pop punk, alternative, emo and more genres. Past performers include Blink-182, No Doubt, Sublime, Beck, Katy Perry, NOFX, Limp Bizkit, Black Eyed Peas, Green Day, Eminem, Yellowcard, Bad Religion and more.

'Woman Unknown' and 'Minotaur' also picked up trophies at the film festival honoring cinematography.

Fatherland and Wild Horse Nine were among the top honorees at the 34th Camerimage Film Festival, held in Toruń, Poland, which celebrates cinematography.

During Saturday’s closing ceremony for the festival that changed its name earlier this year to ToruńCamerimage, Fatherland cinematographer Lukasz Zal was awarded the Golden Frog for the main competition, with director Pawel Pawlikowski’s film picking up momentum as an Academy Award contender in the category. Representing Poland’s selection for the international feature Oscar, Fatherland centers on Nobel Prize-winning author Thomas Mann (played by Hanns Zischler) and daughter Erika (Sandra Hüller) taking a road trip through Germany amid the Cold War. Cinematographer Jasper J. Spanning won the Silver Frog for director May El-Toukhy’s Woman Unknown, while Mikhail Krichman was awarded the Bronze Frog for director Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur.

The audience award went to director Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine, shot by Ben Davis. John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell star in the comedic spy thriller that holds major Oscar aspirations.

For the Cinematographers’ Debuts competition, the Golden Frog went to Eira Wyn Jones for Effi O Blaenau from director Tereza Nvotova. Kaifeng Zhong collected the Directors’ Debuts Golden Frog for Atlantic Rhapsody.

In the nonfiction categories, the Golden Frog for Documentary Features competition went to Eva Kraljevic for director Petar Glomazic’s To Hold a Mountain. For the Documentary Shorts competition, Maxim Arbugaev and Vladimir Egorov picked up the Golden Frog for director Evgenia Arbugaeva’s Chuuraa.

For the TV Series Competition, cinematographer Maciej Sobieraj was awarded the Golden Frog for Silent Night, helmed by Jan Holoubek. The Golden Frog in the Music Videos Competition went to Jeff Bierman for director (LA)HORDE’s “What You Want.”

In Poland’s national race, cinematographer Alan Ruczyński collected the Golden Frog for his work on directors Eliza Godlewska and Alan Ruczyński’s A Free Woman.

Closing out the ceremony was the Film and Art School Etudes Competition, with cinematographer Francesca Avanzini claiming the Golden Tadpole for director Paoli de Luca’s Revolver. Paul Ader picked up the Silver Tadpole for Konstantin Münzel’s Nika’s Room. Enrico Barbaro Jr. received the Bronze Tadpole for Marco Araujo’s Until We Bury Them!

"It’s amazing that by using radio wavelengths, we can detect the storms on a star over 5,000 light-years away."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Astronomers have traced a mysterious radio signal back to a cosmic odd couple comprised of a dead star, a white dwarf, and its stellar companion, a sun-like star.

The white dwarf in the newly discovered system, designated GPM J071507−114153 and located around 5,000 light-years away, spins once every eight minutes, sending out radio pulses. These radio pulses have been seen from binary systems with smaller and cooler red dwarf stars before, but rarely from a system like GPM J071507−114153.

GPM J071507−114153 belongs to a class of celestial objects called long-period transients (LPTs) known to produce radio signals that switch on and off over intervals of minutes or hours. Around a dozen LPTs have been detected since the team behind this research found the first in 2021. Several previously discovered LPT systems contain a white dwarf and a companion star, but it has been unclear which of the two stars was generating the radio pulses. That means the discovery of GPM J071507−114153 and finding that the pulses come from close to the white dwarf could be a significant step toward understanding the nature of LPTs.

"This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion," team leader and commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKA), Sam McSweeney, said in a statement. "So we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself."

The pulses seen by the team also allowed them to detect stellar flares erupting on the sun-like star.

"As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a 'stellar prominence,' which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star's surface," team member Natasha Hurley-Walker of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR), Curtin University, Australia, said. "It's amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5,000 light-years away."

Hurley-Walker and the team at ICRAR have been at the cutting edge of rare star systems like this.

"We detected this system in a large survey using the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia," Hurley-Walker said. "We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position."

After the radio telescopes detected this LPT, it was confirmed using the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea in Hawaii. The visible light follow-up of Keck also confirmed that the star in GPM J071507−114153 was a G-type star, just like the sun.

MeerKAT and the MWA are both precursors for the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), the world’s largest and most sensitive radio telescope project. That means the future is bright for LPTs.

"If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKA telescopes are completely built," McSweeney said.

The team's research was published on Thursday (Nov. 12) in the journal Nature Astronomy.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

#738. Inside the Plane Where Simple Plan, Hoobastank and More Performed Mid-Flight as Planes Were Grounded Across the U.S.

The Hollywood Reporter had a prime seat for the once-in-a-lifetime event on a Southwest plan — which took off about an hour before all planes were grounded by the FAA — that also featured The Used and Lolo.

Have you ever been serenaded at 35,000 feet by Hoobastank? We’re betting that answer is no.

But about 125 lucky Southwest Airline passengers got that opportunity on Friday on a charted Southwest Airlines flight from Los Angeles to headed to the Vans Warped Tour in Orlando.

The festivities actually kicked off that morning in Terminal 1 of LAX. At the gate, guests — who were mostly dressed in black, rock-themed attire, with plenty donning sort of Vans apparel, from shoes to purses to hats — were greeted with a rock music playlist as passengers had the opportunity to perform their favorites. (Shout-out to the woman named Gianna who gave a high-energy performance of Fall Out Boy’s “Sugar, We’re Goin Down.”) Then they were invited to a meet-and-greet with recording artists Lolo, Simple Plan, Hoobastank and The Used, all of whom are were on the Vans Warped Tour lineup. Related Stories Movies 'Fatherland' Wins Top Camerimage Prize as 'Wild Horse Nine' Nabs Audience Award TV Philomena Cunk Comes for Hollywood

What some of the passengers — who included fans, influences and journalists — didn’t realize is that all four acts were going to perform on the flight to Orlando. The initiative is part of the airline’s Live at 35, an in-flight entertainment program — celebrating its 15th anniversary this year — that surprises passengers with live pop-up music performances and events at 35,000 feet.

Once in the air, singer Lolo kicked things off somewhere over Texas with a four-song set. At one point, Lolo shared that she “almost didn’t take the gig because I’m a nervous flier and this is the longest I’ve gone without wearing a seat belt.” (Incidentally, the flight took off about an hour before the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all U.S. flights “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” The buzz on the plane was that our flight was likely one of very few planes in the air at the time.)

The aforementioned Hoobastank performed a trio of sings, culminating with their 2004 smash hit “The Reason.” During that song, lead singer Doug Robb asked the flight staff to turn off all the lights and the passengers to turn on their cell flashlights, upping the concert vibe inside the aircraft. The passengers also took part in a rousing sing-along to the tune.

“Is this the most annoying flight you’ve ever been on?” Robb joked. Walking through the plane, he swiped an iPad from a passenger who was evidently doing some online shopping. “I think you should buy that,” he joked.

During his set, The Used frontman Bert McCracken noted the unusual “venue” as the flight was passing over New Orleans. “This is the weirdest fucking shit I’ve ever done in my life,” he quipped. The band played four songs, and also turned “The Taste of Ink” into a sing-along. (“Everyone knows the lyrics to this song. It’s called ‘The Reason,'” McCracken joked in a callback to Hoobastank’s crowd-participation performance.)

Simple Plan’s Pierre Bouvier took the stage — floor? aisle? — last, performing songs including “I’d Do Anything.” After the song, he joked, “Give it up for Mark Hoppus,” the Blink-182 singer-bassist who is featured on the song. (Hoppus was not present.)

Bouvier joked it was “super awkward” to perform on a plane, even changing the lyrics to “I’d do anything for you, Vans Warped Tour,” before giving a knowing look and quipping, “Really, anything.” Bouvier also sang “I’m Just a Kid,” noting that it went viral on social media several years after its release as part of the #ImJustAKidChallenge Challenge, where users re-created childhood photographs as adults or adolescents.

As the plane began descending, Bouvier asked the flight crew to turn down the lights, quipping that “the flight crew didn’t know they were going to become the light crew.”

Markus Lloyd is the host for these events, which have featured acts including Julian Marley (son of Bob), the Plain White T’s, Magic!, Shane Smith & The Saints, Barenaked Ladies, Imagine Dragons, Chris Young and Cassidy Pope. “What’s fun” about these experiences, he told THR, “is that when we’re heading someplace fun, like the Vans Warped Tour, or Vegas, the plane has already kind of turned up a bit. And so when you tell them they’re getting this extra thing, it’s like they won the lottery. They’re like, ‘Oh my gosh, I’m going to Vegas AND I get a concert in the place? And that’s when we go, ‘You can’t get this anywhere besides Southwest.'”

For an encore on Friday’s flight, Hoobastank got up to perform one last song just moments before the flight landed safely in Orlando.

"Martian Isolation" is an upcoming single-player, first-person survival horror game that's just been revealed with a suitably creepy launch trailer. And yes, it does look an awful lot like "The Martian," doesn't it?

There's a lot of survival gameplay on display here that mirrors Mark Watney's tale of survival on the Red Planet, as your stranded protagonist is forced to explore the Martian surface to acquire resources, grow plants, and repair their base.

That comparison to Andy Weir's sci-fi masterpiece does fall away as you get further into the trailer, though, when the horror part of the game's description comes into play: Flickering lights, creepy figures stalking the halls of your Martian habitat, and blood dripping from the walls.

Oh yeah, that's some good creepy sci-fi horror right there. It's giving "Event Horizon", and that's always getting a thumbs-up from me.

There's no release date scheduled at this time, with the 'Martian Isolation' Steam page simply listing it as "coming soon," though the YouTube trailer description does say it "will be available on Steam in 2027".

You can't pre-order yet, but if this looks like your jam, you can add it to your wishlist.

Beyond that, we know shockingly little about this title. It's the debut game from Golden Milestone Studio, but there's very little information out there beyond a name. The latest blog post on the game's Steam page says that they're a "small team," but what we've seen so far is encouraging.

There seems to be a pronounced split between the survival and horror elements of the game along the day/night cycle. Daytime sees you exploring the Martian surface, smashing rocks, cleaning solar panels, and doing sick jumps on a quad bike.

The psychological torment only begins once the sun goes down (they mostly come out at night … mostly), as your character starts encountering cosmic horrors and weird naked zombie men.

Are they hallucinations, or is there some malevolent presence hiding in the blood-red sands of Mars?

I'm always looking for new ways to shatter my psyche and possibly soil my pants, so I'll be keeping a close eye on this one. In the meantime, I do need to get back and finish "Routine." I left my character hiding under a desk months ago, and I haven't been brave enough to go back. As Mama always said, you can't have any Martian horror until you finish your lunar horror first.
